title: US ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy comes into effect as trade war drags on
description: A US ban on several Canadian imports, including alcohol, dairy and motorcycles, has come into effect as a trade war between the two neighbours drags o
body: A US ban on several Canadian imports, including alcohol, dairy and motorcycles, has come into effect as a trade war between the two neighbours drags on.The latest measure by the Trump administration is in response to Canada's  implementation of tariffs on a range of US goods earlier this month following a breakdown in trade talks. Canada is not expected to retaliate further, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying earlier this month that the impact the import bans will have on Canada's economy is "modest". Trade talks remain on ice, with US trade representative Jamieson Greer telling CNBC recently that President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with his current relationship with Canada."They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side," Greer said of relations with Canada in an interview with the US network last week.Tuesday's trade ban applies to nearly C$1bn ($710m; £530m) worth of Canadian liquor exported to the US, as well as whey products used in protein powder. Motorcycle exports to the US will also be impacted, though Canada only sent about 5,000 motorcycles south of the border in 2025 that were worth about C$120m, according to national data by Statistics Canada, meaning the impact would be limited. The import bans were first announced by Trump in a series of executive orders signed on 8 September. In them, Trump said the measures are in response to "continued discrimination" by Canada on US dairy, automotives and alcohol.  Speaking to reports on Monday, he accused Canada of "treating the United States very unfairly"."They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world," Trump said.Carney said earlier this month that the bans "are relatively modest measures" when compared to other trade actions the US has imposed on Canada. He acknowledged, however, that the bans will hurt certain businesses and sectors that are directly targeted.Derek Holt, an economist with Canadian bank Scotiabank, wrote in an analysis that "these actions are face-saving by the US administration, not substantive in nature and that's a positive". About 93% of all Canadian liquor exports in 2025 were sold to the US. Spirits Canada, a group representing Canadian liquor producers, has said the consequences to the industry "could be significant"., externalEconomists and businesses have also warned that the bans will add uncertainty to the future of Canada's trade relationship with the US, its largest trade partner. In addition to these latest import bans, the US has imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, including dairy, alcohol, steel and aluminium products, as well as 25% tariffs on Canadian-built cars. Canada in return has placed retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on more than 700 US products, as well as a 25% levy on certain steel and aluminium products. Most Canadian provinces have also stopped selling US liquor. Tariffs - taxes paid on imported goods - are central to Trump's economic agenda, who argues that they raise government revenue and encourage consumers to buy American-made goods.Economists, however, argue that they have raised prices of everyday goods for consumers and have disrupted the global economy.

schema.headline: US ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy comes into effect as trade war drags on

title: Christa Pike execution: Tennessee governor rejects clemency plea
description: "After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike's request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of t
body: "After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike's request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene," Governor Lee said in a statement.Pike's legal team had filed the clemency petition earlier this month, requesting that her death sentence be commuted to life in prison.Moving ahead with Pike's execution puts Tennessee "on singular footing", her attorneys said, as she would be the first person the state "executes in the modern death penalty era who was a teenager at the time of the offence".Attorneys Stephen Ferrell, Kelly Gleason and Randy Spivey said the governor's decision "leaves unanswered vital questions about Tennessee's execution protocol"."With this decision, the State of Tennessee is ignoring what both science and our legal system have decided: an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain, and 18 is too young to face execution," they said in a statement on Monday.The murder of Colleen Slemmer created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the 19-year-old was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.A year later, she was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, while then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp- who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.At the time of her incarceration, the 21-year-old was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.Pike is scheduled to be executed on 30 September after years of failed appeals.Colleen's mother has insisted she wants Pike's execution to move forward so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

schema.headline: Christa Pike execution: Tennessee governor rejects clemency plea

title: New York Times executive fatally shot by elderly in-laws, police say
description: A New York Times executive was fatally shot in California, allegedly by his wife's elderly parents who have been arrested on suspicion of murder.Jonat
body: A New York Times executive was fatally shot in California, allegedly by his wife's elderly parents who have been arrested on suspicion of murder.Jonathan McKinsey, 40, the newspaper's director of engineering for games player experience, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in a car park in Dublin - 35 miles (56km) east of San Francisco - on Saturday afternoon, police said.Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, his parents-in-law who are both 77 years old, are facing multiple charges, including first-degree murder.It was unclear whether the couple have a lawyer, and they are due to appear in court to formally face the charges on Wednesday. McKinsey's death was confirmed by The New York Times.His body was found at 15:00 (23:00 GMT) on Thursday afternoon outside the Dublin Sports Grounds.Witnesses told KGO-TV in San Francisco that they heard a flurry of gunshots, before seeing the victim on the ground."I saw the guy drop to the floor: head bloody and chest bloody," witness Assad Razawi told the news outlet. His daughter added that her father saw the couple "walking together and then casually walk away from the shooting".The couple were arrested several minutes later by an officer passing by the scene. They had remained in the area after the attack, a witness said.McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police. Police have not disclosed  any motive for his killing.The elderly couple are being held at the Santa Rita jail.They also face charges of felony conspiracy, wilful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence, and child endangerment.

schema.headline: New York Times executive fatally shot by elderly in-laws, police say

title: Turkey stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan
description: An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but
body: An Istanbul court has convicted a popular comedian of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan – and handed down a sentence of almost 19 months – but ordered his release due to time served. It has also placed him under a travel ban, preventing him from travelling outside Turkey.A final decision in the case will come from the court of appeals.Deniz Göktaş - who denied the charges - has already spent nearly 90 days in prison. Prosecutors had asked for up to 12 years. His case comes amid a wave of arrests in Turkey that human rights groups say is aimed at crushing dissent.His stand-up routine went viral on YouTube, attracting more than 15 million views.Prosecutors had singled out a line in which the comedian called the Turkish leader "a shy dictator", but Göktaş insisted there was "no criminal element" in his comments. "Dictator is not an insult," he said, "it is a political characterisation."But angering the president in Turkey is not funny. Göktaş was arrested and handcuffed at Istanbul airport in July when he returned from a holiday.During his court appearance on Monday, it was clear he did not lose his sense of humour during his 88 days in solitary confinement."Three months have been taken away from my life," he said on the stand. "But I quit smoking, so I'll add another three months to my life." That drew laughter and loud applause in court.Outside, supporters like Firat Aksal – a fellow comedian – were very pleasantly surprised by the verdict.   "We hardly know what to do with our happiness," he said. "We are thrilled. To be honest we weren't hopeful of getting a fair trial. "Göktaş was released at 21:45 local time (18:45 GMT) and greeted by well-wishers, including his parents who he was seen hugging, outside a prison facility.Aksal said Göktaş would now rest for a few days, and see his family, and then return to the stage.After his release, Göktaş told reporters: "I'm very happy to be reunited with my family, mother, father, and friends."But he added: "There are thousands of other people in prisons across Turkey. Some, like me, are being held in pre-trial detention, while others have been convicted because of their views. "So, of course, it's wonderful to be out. I've missed it very much. But there is not much difference between inside and outside. I hope the day comes when we can all regain our freedom together."Many others remain behind bars, including journalists, human rights campaigners, student protesters, LGBTQ activists, and the elected Mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu. Prisons are full in Turkey these days.Erdogan and his party in the past have denied arrests, such as that of Imamoglu, have been politically motivated, insisting that Turkey's judiciary is independent.Additional reporting by Gunce Akpamuk

schema.headline: Turkey stand-up comic released after being convicted of insulting Erdoğan

title: Hurricane Polo makes landfall in Mexico, with life-threatening winds and flooding
description: Hurricane Polo has made landfall along the northern Pacific coast of Mexico, lashing the state of Baja California Sur with life-threatening winds and
body: Hurricane Polo has made landfall along the northern Pacific coast of Mexico, lashing the state of Baja California Sur with life-threatening winds and heavy rain that has already flooded some coastal areas.Mexican officials said Polo moved ashore just south of the surfing and fishing village of Las Barrancas bringing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h). Polo is moving northeast and on the forecast track, its core is predicted to continue passing over Baja California Sur before moving inland over the southern part of the Mexican state of Sonora later on Tuesday.Residents in threatened areas have been encouraged to seek shelter.Shopkeeper María Palomino, 57, spent the night at a high school which has been turned into a temporary shelter. "If something happens, it's better to come to the shelter," she told AFP news agency.A whale-watching and fishing guide who was boarding up the facade of his home told AFP the storm was "coming with full force".The US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) said that while Polo was expected to weaken as it moved over the Baja California peninsula, it was forecast to still be at hurricane strength when it makes its second landfall in mainland Mexico. Meteorologists said Polo could dump between 6 and 12 inches (150-300mm) of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, which they warned could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.The NHC said a storm surge was also expected to produce significant coastal flooding in areas of onshore winds. "Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves," it said in an update.Even before Polo made landfall, residents said there were power cuts in Baja California Sur. US media reported some flooding in the fishing town of Puerto San Carlos and the Associated Press said waves crested sea barriers in the area, where many residents had been evacuated due to the threat.

schema.headline: Hurricane Polo makes landfall in Mexico, with life-threatening winds and flooding

title: Malaysia begins controversial repatriation of asylum seekers to Myanmar
description: The Malaysian government has started repatriating around 5,000 asylum seekers from Myanmar, under a controversial deal agreed with Myanmar's military
body: The Malaysian government has started repatriating around 5,000 asylum seekers from Myanmar, under a controversial deal agreed with Myanmar's military ruler Min Aung Hlaing.Three ships from the Myanmar navy are scheduled to leave Malaysia later today carrying the first 1,476 returnees.Human rights groups have condemned the repatriation, saying the returnees face violence, persecution and forced conscription into the Myanmar army.Malaysia has described the repatriation as voluntary, but has barred the UN refugee agency from seeing or screening the returnees, who have been kept in detention centres.According to Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, these returnees will include Rohingyas: a persecuted Muslim minority who have sought sanctuary in Malaysia in large numbers after being driven out of Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens. Anwar, whose popularity has fallen sharply this year, says he is responding to growing public hostility towards the large Rohingya population in Malaysia and has no choice but to negotiate with the Myanmar government over their return.But the move signals a striking shift in attitude. Anwar, a former political prisoner, has previously presented himself as a defender of human rights and freedom, and called for more to be done to help the Rohingyas. Under him, Malaysia has refused to recognise Min Aung Hlaing's regime, and has been one of the strongest voices in South East Asia pushing for a negotiated end to Myanmar's civil war.What has changed?Two things. First, increased economic strain on lower-income Malaysians since the Covid pandemic, which has stirred resentment of the Rohingyas.Second, the febrile state of Malaysian politics since 2018, when a historic election unseated the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the ethnic Malay party which had monopolised power for more than 60 years, leading to a revolving door of unstable coalition governments.For many years there was strong public sympathy among Malaysians for their fellow Muslims in Myanmar. In August 2017, a brutal campaign by the Myanmar military drove three quarters of a million Rohingyas out of their homes in Rakhine State and into neighbouring Bangladesh. In the years since, dire conditions in Bangladeshi refugee camps have driven those with enough money to make the perilous sea journey to Malaysia in search of sanctuary and work. While the Malaysian navy and coastguard have long tried to block Rohingya boats from landing in Malaysia, many gotten in via other routes, and for a long time were tolerated. More than 200,000 are now believed to live there, most eking out basic livings from manual labour.Sentiment among Malaysians started to shift during the pandemic, which hit the country's economy hard. At a time of heightened public fear over the new coronavirus, accusations against Rohingya migrants spread on social media, with demands for their deportation. In response, the then-government hardened its attitude, saying Malaysia could accept no more refugees and ordering raids on communities believed to be harbouring illegal immigrants.Much the same has happened in 2026. In May, an online complaint claimed that Rohingyas had failed to dispose of animal waste properly after the Muslim Eid al Adha festival, igniting a viral social media campaign falsely accusing Rohingya leaders of demanding land and citizenship in Malaysia. Shortly thereafter, an online petition on Change.org calling for Rohingyas to be kicked out of Malaysia received more than 400,000 signatures, before being taken down.Given Anwar's one-time reputation as a champion of liberal values, he might have been expected to push back against this wave of hate and disinformation. He has said the Rohingyas should be treated humanely. "We can arrest them, but do not beat, intimidate or humiliate them," he said in a recent podcast interview - although this is exactly what human rights groups have accused Malaysian officials of doing in immigration detention centres. Nonetheless, Anwar insists that the Rohingya must be expelled. "They have clearly become a burden," he said in the same interview. "A security burden, an economic burden and a source of hostility among the people."Some of his former supporters have accused him of betraying his principles. The former head of the Malaysian Anti Corruption Commission, Latheefa Koya, says his decision is "disgraceful, amoral, and shames the nation in the eyes of the international community".Anwar, though, is under great political pressure. Once described as a perpetual prime minister-in-waiting, he finally got the top job in 2022, but only by forming an uneasy coalition with his one-time adversaries UMNO. Since then he has seen his own popularity plunge and his party lose seats in recent local elections. He must call a general election by early 2028."He is in a corner, at his weakest point", says Tricia Yeoh, Director of the Asian Institute for Policy and Engagement at the University of Nottingham Malaysia."He has been forced to make concessions to his UMNO partners... There have been several corruption scandals, and his own party is divided. And after four years of telling voters this is what is required to maintain his fragile coalition, they are no longer willing to go along with that narrative."Instead, Yeoh says, ethnic Malays, who make up more than half of the electorate, are responding to the well-trodden UMNO narrative that they need special support and protection from the state - the kind of racial politics which she says feeds fear and resentment of outsiders. "It's the same narrative you hear in the rest of the world, about immigrants taking jobs, that we should not be spending our public funds on facilities for them."However, it is not clear how any Rohingyas can be repatriated to Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens.Rohingyas are not permitted to travel inside Myanmar, and are only allowed to live in Rakhine State, which borders Bangladesh. But nearly all of Rakhine State is now under the control of the insurgent Arakan Army, and subject to sustained bombardment by the Myanmar air force. On Monday, the day before the repatriation, the Arakan Army said two bombs killed 49 people at a market in the town of Kyauktaw.The only place Rohingyas could conceivably be returned to is the state capital Sittwe - but it is besieged and isolated, and even there Rohingyas are confined to wretched camps which are critically short of food and medicine. Rights groups also fear that any men in the group could be forcibly conscripted into the army to fight in the civil war. Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have explained how these formidable obstacles can be overcome, nor how their planned repatriation can be consistent with humanitarian principles."We all dream of being able to return home one day," said Nur Sadek, a Rohingya refugee rights advocate, "but we want to return because it is safe and because we choose to — not because we are forced to. "For me, the most important thing is that Rohingya and other refugees affected by this decision are listened to and treated with dignity."

schema.headline: Malaysia begins controversial repatriation of asylum seekers to Myanmar

title: French PM Lecornu warns against escalation of school protests
description: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", f
body: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", following the arrests of 164 people on Monday. The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockading their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."But a French union that defends the interests of high school students said the protests were a "legitimate response" to the conditions they face.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 12 members of the security forces, 12 students and three school staff were injured on Monday, while 180 schools were affected.He did not provide further details on those who had been arrested. The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.Incidents of vandalism were reported, along with fireworks being aimed at police,  and the protests have now spread to other regions in France. According to the AFP news agency, four high schools were reported to have been blockaded in the southern regions of Alpes-Maritimes and Var. Protests have also been reported in Marseille, the northern Lille area and Sedan in the north-eastern Ardennes.The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, defended the protests in a post on social media. "Lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classes, stress caused by Parcoursup [the web platform used in France for students to apply to the first year of higher education]... These issues are by no means inevitable, but simply the result of 10 years of Macron's policies and the lack of resources in the national education system," it said.It called on students to blockade schools on Tuesday in defence of "their rights and against budget austerity".On the same day, unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants also called for a day of walkouts to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions.In response to the student movement, Lecornu said "the difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed", but that "violence must be condemned unequivocally, and its perpetrators must answer for their actions".The prime minister also accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of urging students to expand the movement.Jean-Luc Mélenchon, LFI's leader, blamed the Lecornu government for having "ordered the crackdown" on the protest, adding that the high school students taking part were "harmless".But Nuñez said the demonstrations and blockades were "not very typical protest movements"."It is much more like urban violence, with a number of individuals who were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes, equipped with projectiles, who clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces," he said."It wasn't about making demands; it was really violence in its purest form."Since the protests began, several incidents involving violence between students and police officers have been reported.In one incident, a police officer reportedly fired a round from a grenade launcher used for crowd control, injuring a high school student, according to France's BFMTV.Investigations have been launched into these incidents, the broadcaster added.

schema.headline: French PM Lecornu warns against escalation of school protests

title: US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University
description: ByKayla Epstein and Nardine SaadNew York state prosecutors say they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell Univers
body: ByKayla Epstein and Nardine SaadNew York state prosecutors say they will reopen a criminal inquiry into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024.The woman filed a civil lawsuit on 16 September alleging she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house at the university."Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means possible" through a grand jury, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said Monday.Cornell University said that while it supported the case being brought before a grand jury, "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false".The woman, referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges in her lawsuit that on the night of 19 October 2024, seven men from Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity chapter allegedly assaulted her in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine. Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and was incapable of providing consent.She said she reported the incident to Cornell University Police on 8 November 2024. The lawsuit also contains an image purported to be from a Snapchat fraternity group chat, in which a participant alerted other members, in vulgar terms, to the potential for a sexual encounter with Jane Doe.Van Houten said on Monday that at the time of the assault two years ago, his office concluded that evidence from her statement to authorities did not meet the legal threshold to bring charges.He said he reached out to Jane Doe and her lawyers for more information as he prepared to bring the case to a grand jury.In the US legal system, prosecutors convene grand juries to weigh evidence and testimony and eventually vote on whether they merit criminal charges.In his statement, Van Houten included a summary of what Jane Doe told the Cornell University Police Department in 2024 after the alleged attack. He noted the statement differed from the allegations laid out in the lawsuit."Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped," Van Houten said in a statement on Monday."On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."Van Houten added that Jane Doe's lawyers had never been in touch with him to say her original statement was inaccurate or to ask him to reconsider his decision not to bring charges.He later acknowledged "the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them".The BBC has contacted Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. In a statement on Monday obtained by CBS, the BBC's US partner, he said: "In the days following the assault, [Jane Doe] was traumatised, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode."Giuffra said Jane Doe never spoke to anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint, adding: "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations.""The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognise that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them," he said.Jane Doe also alleged in her civil lawsuit that Cornell did not protect her nor adequately punish the men involved, alleging they were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays". Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the incident and the university's handling, the suit states, adding that news of the incident quickly circulated through the school.  In November 2024, Cornell University issued a public statement regarding the "serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house", saying its campus police department was investigating and that it had suspended the local chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, as well as "a number of students."Cornell also said it had opened an internal investigation as well as a civil rights inquiry under the Title IX law - which bars sex discrimination in schools that receive funding from the federal government, including most universities.The Xi chapter of Chi Phi  fraternity remains barred from its campus, Cornell said.On Monday, the university disputed Jane Doe's allegation that it did not adequately investigate or punish the alleged perpetrators.The university said in a statement that the matter was referred to a "panel of trained faculty and staff" that issued "a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell"."None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," Cornell said.Jeremy Saland, an attorney for one of the men named in the lawsuit, denied the allegations.Saland acknowledged his client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat", but "did nothing else." Saland denied his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine".The case has received national attention following Doe's lawsuit and the announcement the case would be reopened. Several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, and US lawmaker Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have spoken out about it. There is a mix of outrage and shock on campus, along with "a humungous wave of solidarity" from people across the US,  Sophia Dasser, editor-in-chief of the student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, told the BBC.The newspaper's editorial board published the names of the men named in the lawsuit and called for an independent, third-party review of the reporting and resolution processes."Much of the frustration, in my opinion, does stem from how little students really were told over the last two years regarding this case and how opaque the Title IX process is," Dasser said. She noted that other universities publicise anonymous outcome, sanction and process results of sexual assaults on campus, but Cornell University does not."So all we ask is really, truly transparency to the student body, especially the student body in which the university is responsible for keeping safe," she said.The mayor of Ithaca, New York, where Cornell is located, has called for a moratorium on all student event and special event permits. The pause is in place until the university "conducts an accounting of its protocols to prevent and prosecute crimes of sexual violence".The Ivy League institution on Monday said that a task force on campus sexual assault was formed in 2025 and has made recommendations that have either been implemented or are in development. A 2025 school survey, external found that 35% of undergraduate women and 8% of undergraduate men  have reported experiencing sexual assault during their time at Cornell, the report said. The report said that despite a long history of actions to address sexual assault, rates of sexual assault "remain persistently high".If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide., externalA list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: US prosecutors reopen case of alleged gang rape at Cornell University

title: Evicted Spanish pensioner, Maricarmen Abascal, can move home, lawyer says
description: An evicted elderly disabled woman, who has become symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her l
body: An evicted elderly disabled woman, who has become symbolic of Spain's housing crisis, will be able to return to her home in Madrid, according to her lawyer.Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September. She was admitted to hospital after the eviction.Her eviction has led to widespread anger across Spain, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has promised housing relief measures when his cabinet meets on Tuesday.Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told a press conference there had been "goodwill from both parties" and that she would pay a similar amount of rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.Duro had met the investment company Urbagestión, which owns the apartment, for several hours on Monday, and the agreement they reached still has to be approved by Maricarmen Abascal, as she was unable to take part in the meeting.She added that Abascal, who is being treated for exhaustion, would sign the deal when she felt better.Up to 1,000 protesters welcomed the agreement at Madrid's Puerta del Sol, where hundreds of tents have been set up. However, the city's Tenants' Union has called on the government to approve deeper housing reforms "so that there are no more Maricarmens".The tent protest has been criticised by Madrid regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who has accused the government of failing to respond in time to Spain's housing shortage and of now coming up with "sectarian" and "deeply ideological" proposals."I'm merely asking to be told at what age I can stop paying my landlords so I can stay in my place, and maybe I'll even join the next tenants' protest," she said.Spain needed a million more homes to address demographic growth encouraged by the Sánchez government itself, she added.Maricarmen Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020). The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 however she was still unable to pay this with her monthly pension of €1,350.Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts.Her case triggered nationwide protests and tens of thousands of people to march through the Spanish capital on Saturday to object to the eviction and to demand stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.Duro said the agreement, yet to be signed, was the "result of the social mobilisation". Supporters called it a victory but promised to continue their fight to prevent similar evictions, and to press for more affordable housing.The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents. It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.8 per square metre (£20.4) and €22.7 per square metre respectively.Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party, which lacks a majority in Parliament, is hoping to agree a new decree with his political allies to appease public outrage.A council of ministers was due to meet on Tuesday morning, with left-wing ministers calling for permanent protection for tenants.Negotiations went on through the night and the left-wing Catalan party ERC is said to have called for a halt to all evictions involving vulnerable people while also demanding a hike on taxes for tourist accommodation.In a speech on Monday evening, Sánchez promised that the government would act responsibly to tackle the "housing emergency suffered by so many people"."Patriotism also means preventing an 87-year-old woman from ending up on the street after a lifetime in her home," he said.

schema.headline: Evicted Spanish pensioner, Maricarmen Abascal, can move home, lawyer says

title: Burkina Faso's Ibrahim Traoré opens first gold refinery in Ouagadougou
description: With gold production on the rise, Traoré's government set up a state-owned mining company two years ago.Foreign mining firms are now required to give
body: With gold production on the rise, Traoré's government set up a state-owned mining company two years ago.Foreign mining firms are now required to give the state a 15% stake in their operations and train local workers.The World Gold Council said output rose by 17% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, helped by increased production at several mines.But successive governments have struggled to regulate the country's extensive artisanal and small-scale mining industry, where smuggling and informal trading have made it difficult for the authorities to account for all the gold produced.The government has also alleged that some illegally traded gold helps finance the Islamist insurgency that has engulfed much of the country.Burkina Faso has been fighting armed Islamist groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State for years, with large areas outside full government control.The new refinery, known as Raffinor-BF, cost more than 11bn CFA francs ($19m; £14m), according to the presidency.It said the project was financed by the state, including through the National Precious Metals Company (Sonasp), in partnership with Burkina Faso's private sector.The plant will initially be capable of refining 164 tonnes of gold a year, significantly more than the country's current annual production. The government says its eventual capacity could rise to 515 tonnes, suggesting it also wants the refinery to process gold from elsewhere in the region."This is the day we take back the keys to our own house,"  Mines Minister Yacouba Zabré Gouba said at the opening."Our gold will no longer be used to create added value for others while our people remain in need."The refinery is the latest element of Capt Traoré's drive to increase state control over Burkina Faso's natural resources and reduce its economic dependence on foreign companies and former Western partners.Since taking power in a coup in September 2022, the 38-year-old army captain has promoted a nationalist economic agenda centred on domestic production and greater control of strategic industries.His government has increased state involvement in the mining sector and has sought to reorganise the trade in artisanal gold.The authorities suspended exports of gold produced by artisanal and semi-mechanised mines in 2024, saying the move was intended to better regulate the sector.Capt Traoré has previously accused smugglers of taking large quantities of gold out of Burkina Faso illegally and said some of the proceeds were helping finance militant groups.The refinery also forms part of a broader government campaign to process more commodities domestically rather than exporting them in raw form.Traoré has presented such projects as evidence of Burkina Faso becoming more economically self-reliant, alongside investments in industries including cotton, textiles and food processing.His policies have coincided with historically high international gold prices and increased global production. Worldwide mine output reached an estimated record 3,672 tonnes in 2025, according to the World Gold Council.Burkina Faso's government says the new plant should eventually be capable of refining all the gold produced by both its industrial mines and artisanal miners.Several West African countries are also seeking to process more of their gold at home.Guinea and Ghana have restricted exports of unrefined gold, while Mali is building its first refinery with help of a Russian firm. Ivory Coast also plans to open a refinery next year.

schema.headline: Burkina Faso's Ibrahim Traoré opens first gold refinery in Ouagadougou

title: South Korea summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row
description: South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador after President Volodymyr Zelensky last week announced his government had transferred two capture
body: South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador after President Volodymyr Zelensky last week announced his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo lodged a formal complaint with Andrii Vieshkin and expressed "strong regret" that Zelensky had revealed the transfer, which Seoul says was supposed to be a secret.The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.President Lee Jae Myung called the disclosure "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.Ukraine's foreign ministry declined to comment when approached by the BBC.In early 2025, Ukraine said its forces had captured two North Korean soldiers as prisoners of war in Russia's Kursk Oblast.After more than a year of negotiations between Seoul and Kyiv, Zelensky announced they had been transferred to South Korea at the UN General Assembly last Wednesday - adding they had not been "easy to capture alive".Seoul confirmed the news but sharply criticised Zelensky for allegedly breaking an agreement to keep the transfer a secret.This was partly to protect the North Koreans' families, President Lee's office said in a statement, which added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.Seoul demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.Lee faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure. The South Korean opposition accused him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.Lee, whose party takes a conciliatory approach to the North, has been making efforts to reopen peace talks, with little success.Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks."When North Korea actively participates in a war in Europe, South Korea cannot remain a distant observer," said Mykhailo Podolyak, a senior adviser to Zelensky. "The transfer of defence technologies and capabilities from Seoul to Kyiv is not just about helping Ukraine; it is about South Korea protecting its own long-term security interests by containing the expansion of an aggressive totalitarian axis."This July, Seoul announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko

schema.headline: South Korea summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row

title: LPU Phagwara: A rape rumour sends an Indian university into turmoil and empties hostels
description: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostelsImage source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Some violent protesters a
body: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostelsImage source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Some violent protesters allegedly torched police cars parked on the highway on Sunday ByZoya Mateen & Azadeh MoshiriBBC News, DelhiOne of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence.Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation.Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack.But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad.Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus.Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised.By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed.University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home.Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate.Image source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests What happened?The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier.The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed.BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered.Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge.Behind the gates, students described a night of fear."We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here."Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here."Image source, BBC PunjabiImage caption, Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence So why have police lodged a case?That the police open a case and investigate the allegation was among the protesters' central demands."The students have been demanding that an FIR  [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC.Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred.Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room."As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said.But they are continuing to examine the footage."The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this."Image source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday Why did the protests grow so large?It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself.There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university."We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield."Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played.Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own.On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them.The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations.Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases.Image source, ANIImage caption, There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest What is happening now?For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians.Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest.The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety.The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed?Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest."I feel students can't do this," she said.Additional reporting by Harmandeep Singh, BBC PunjabiFollow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: LPU Phagwara: A rape rumour sends an Indian university into turmoil and empties hostels

title: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma: The Ugandan journalist who became king amid a succession row
description: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the count
body: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family"."As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute"."No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X. But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan". A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs. According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development."I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend. The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage. His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition."I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

schema.headline: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma: The Ugandan journalist who became king amid a succession row

title: Stuck between superpowers: How Australia navigates the China-US rivalry
description: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalryImage source, ReutersImage caption, China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 202
body: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalryImage source, ReutersImage caption, China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 2024. Relations between the two countries have been rocky in recent yearsByKaty WatsonAustralia correspondent Reporting fromTownsville, North QueenslandSnipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead.Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two.  This is a show of military might." We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan. "Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important."War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation.With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower.But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner.Image source, BBC: Katy WatsonImage caption, Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan says Australia is rehearsing for "the worst type of war"It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight."We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is.Binding tighter to the USThe war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific."We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says.And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500.A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing."Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said. "China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects."The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers.But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties.The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer.Image source, BBC: Katy WatsonImage caption, The Southern Jackaroo exercises are aimed at improving defence cooperation in the Indo-PacificBut that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US."Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll. "Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States."The 'frenemy'While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China.Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner.Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer.Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015.The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs.And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up.A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years.Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges.In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, China is Australia's biggest export marketEven with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary."There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments,"  says Lyons-Jones.This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US.Rise and fall of superpowersEarlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be".Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing."The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says.Image source, PMO AustraliaImage caption, US President Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese. Australians have cooled on their relationship with the US under TrumpBut old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one."This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang.And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act."There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says. "It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

schema.headline: Stuck between superpowers: How Australia navigates the China-US rivalry

title: Ekurhuleni killings: What we know after bodies of 12 women found in South Africa
description: Case 12Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned do
body: Case 12Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken. Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September. The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg. It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

schema.headline: Ekurhuleni killings: What we know after bodies of 12 women found in South Africa
